claim: Mutator alleles have been found at considerable frequencies in populations of infectious and commensal bacteria.
source: Mutator alleles have been found at considerable frequencies in populations of infectious and commensal bacteria (Matic et al., 1997; LeClerc et al., 1996; Oliver et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research on bacterial populations

claim: Mutator alleles have been found at considerable frequencies in populations of viruses.
source: Mutator alleles have been found at considerable frequencies in populations of infectious and commensal bacteria (Matic et al., 1997; LeClerc et al., 1996; Oliver et al., 2000), viruses (Suárez et al., 1992)
evidence: Supported by citation to published research on viral populations

claim: Mutator alleles have been found at considerable frequencies in populations of pathogenic fungi.
source: Mutator alleles have been found at considerable frequencies in populations of infectious and commensal bacteria (Matic et al., 1997; LeClerc et al., 1996; Oliver et al., 2000), viruses (Suárez et al., 1992), and pathogenic fungi (Healey et al., 2016; Billmyre et al., 2017; Boyce et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research on fungal populations

claim: Mutators are believed to be widespread in many cancers.
source: Mutators are also believed to be widespread in many cancers (Loeb, 2011; Lengauer et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on cancer

claim: Mutators have been repeatedly observed to overtake microbial populations during laboratory evolution experiments.
source: have been repeatedly observed to overtake microbial populations during laboratory evolution experiments (Sniegowski et al., 1997; Shaver et al., 2002; Barrick et al., 2009; Notley-McRobb et al., 2002; Pal et al., 2007; Mao et al., 1997; Raynes and Sniegowski, 2014; Voordeckers et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to laboratory evolution studies

claim: Mutator mutations generally do not appear to be inherently advantageous, except potentially in some viruses.
source: mutator mutations generally do not appear to be inherently advantageous (Raynes and Sniegowski, 2014), except potentially in some viruses (Furió et al., 2005; Furió et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on mutator fitness effects

claim: Mutators experience indirect selection mediated by persistent statistical associations with fitness-affecting mutations elsewhere in the genome.
source: Instead, mutators experience indirect selection, mediated by persistent statistical associations with fitness-affecting mutations elsewhere in the genome.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on established population genetics principles

claim: Mutators may invade an adapting population by hitchhiking with linked beneficial mutations even when they have no effect on fitness of their own.
source: As a result, mutators may invade an adapting population by hitchhiking (Smith and Haigh, 1974) with linked beneficial mutations even when they have no effect on fitness of their own (Sniegowski et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on hitchhiking and mutator evolution

claim: Whether or not mutators can successfully hitchhike to fixation has often been described as depending on the initial prevalence of mutator alleles in a population.
source: Whether or not mutators can successfully hitchhike to fixation has often been described as depending on the initial prevalence of mutator alleles in a population - most commonly referred to as frequency or number dependence (Raynes and Sniegowski, 2014; Sniegowski et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to review literature describing this interpretation

claim: It has been proposed that mutators may be expected to invade only when already present in sufficient numbers to produce the successful beneficial mutation first.
source: Accordingly, it has been proposed that mutators may be expected to invade (i.e., are favored by selection) only when already present in sufficient numbers to produce the successful beneficial mutation first, and lose their advantage (i.e., are disfavored by selection) when too rare to do so (reviewed in Raynes and Sniegowski, 2014; Sniegowski et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citations to review literature describing this hypothesis

claim: Mutator strains of E. coli could supplant otherwise isogenic non-mutator strains by hitchhiking with beneficial mutations when initialized above a critical threshold frequency but would decline when initialized below it.
source: Most famously, in a series of pioneering experiments, Lin Chao and colleagues showed that mutator strains of the bacterium E. coli could supplant otherwise isogenic non-mutator strains by hitchhiking with beneficial mutations when initialized above a critical threshold frequency but would decline when initialized below it (Chao and Cox, 1983: reproduced in Figure 1A; Chao et al., 1983)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies and reference to Figure 1A showing the data

claim: A similar pattern of frequency-dependent mutator dynamics has been recapitulated in several other studies in E. coli and S. cerevisiae.
source: Since then, a similar pattern has been recapitulated in several other studies in E. coli and S. cerevisiae (Thompson et al., 2006; Gentile et al., 2011; de Visser and Rozen, 2006; Le Chat et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: A frequency-dependent framing of indirect selection on mutators implies a change in the sign or the strength of indirect selection with frequency.
source: Critically, a frequency-dependent framing of indirect selection on mutators implies a change in the sign or the strength of indirect selection with frequency.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what frequency-dependence means

claim: Indirect selection on mutators is independent of frequency.
source: Here, we use stochastic, agent-based computer simulations to demonstrate that on the contrary, indirect selection on mutators is independent of frequency.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by simulation data presented throughout

claim: Single, randomly-chosen simulation realizations started below a threshold frequency end in mutator loss, while those started above end in fixation.
source: As in Figure 1A, single, randomly-chosen realizations (i.e., simulation replicates) started below a threshold frequency end in mutator loss, while randomly-chosen realizations started above end in fixation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Fixation of an allele in a finite population is a probabilistic process influenced both by selection and random genetic drift.
source: Critically, fixation of an allele in a finite population is a probabilistic process influenced both by selection and random genetic drift
evidence: This is established knowledge in population genetics

claim: Even beneficial mutations will frequently be lost by chance alone.
source: and even beneficial mutations will frequently be lost by chance alone
evidence: This is established knowledge in population genetics about stochastic loss

claim: Whether an allele is truly favored or disfavored by selection can only be ascertained by evaluating its expected behavior averaged across many replicate, independent realizations.
source: As such, whether an allele is truly favored or disfavored by selection can only be ascertained by evaluating its expected behavior averaged across many replicate, independent realizations.
evidence: This is a methodological principle based on statistical reasoning about stochastic processes

claim: When considering the expected mutator frequency averaged across many replicate simulations, the threshold-frequency effect disappears.
source: Indeed, if we consider the expected mutator frequency averaged across many replicate simulations, the threshold-frequency effect disappears (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The transient decline in average mutator frequency reflects selection against the deleterious load inherent to mutators.
source: The transient decline in average frequency seen in Figure 1C reflects selection against the deleterious load inherent to mutators (Kimura, 1967)
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work and reference to data in Figure 1C

claim: Even when mutators are favored, most experimental replicates with rare mutators are expected to end in mutator extinction.
source: Thus even when mutators are favored, most experimental replicates with rare mutators are expected to end in mutator extinction
evidence: This is inferred from the low per-capita fixation probability

claim: All experimental studies that have documented the frequency-based transition included only a few populations at each starting frequency.
source: Indeed, all experimental studies that have documented the frequency-based transition included only a few populations at each starting frequency.
evidence: This is an observation about the design of previous experimental studies

claim: Limited sampling across a broad range of starting frequencies in experiments would explain the sharp transition between fixation at high frequencies and loss at lower ones even when selection is frequency-independent.
source: Such limited sampling across a broad range of starting frequencies in these experiments would explain the sharp transition between fixation at high frequencies and loss at lower ones even when selection is frequency-independent (see also Tanaka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference about how sampling affects observed patterns, supported by citation

claim: The critical frequency-dependent transition observed in experiments is not unique to mutators.
source: In fact, the critical frequency-dependent transition observed in Figure 1A and 1B is not unique to mutators.
evidence: This is demonstrated by showing similar patterns for beneficial mutations in Figure 3

claim: For a directly beneficial mutation, the probability of fixation from low frequencies is relatively low.
source: For example, even for a directly beneficial mutation, the probability of fixation from low frequencies is relatively low (Figure 3A Inset)
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3A Inset

claim: Single realizations of the dynamics of a directly beneficial mutation exhibit a threshold-like switch from fixation to loss.
source: Accordingly, as Figure 3A illustrates, single realizations of the dynamics of a directly beneficial mutation also exhibit a threshold-like switch from fixation to loss.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Expected frequency dynamics of beneficial mutations averaged across many independent realizations confirm that beneficial mutations are favored by selection independent of starting frequency.
source: In contrast, expected frequency dynamics averaged across many independent realizations confirm that beneficial mutations are favored by selection independent of starting frequency (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figure 3B

claim: For mutations under truly frequency-dependent selection, both individual realizations and expected dynamics averaged across many realizations exhibit an actual frequency-dependent transition.
source: Indeed, only for mutations under truly frequency-dependent selection do both the individual realizations (Figure 3C) and the expected dynamics averaged across many realizations (Figure 3D) exhibit an actual frequency-dependent transition.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figures 3C and 3D

claim: Neither the strength nor the sign of selection on mutators depend on initial frequency or number.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that neither the strength nor the sign of selection on mutators depend on initial frequency or number.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the simulation results

claim: In populations favoring higher mutation rates, mutators consistently fare better than the neutral expectation regardless of starting frequency.
source: Instead, we show that in populations favoring higher mutation rates, mutators consistently fare better than the neutral expectation (Figure 1 and Figure 2) regardless of starting frequency.
evidence: Supported by simulation data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: The per-capita probability of mutator fixation remains unchanged with frequency.
source: Most importantly, the per-capita probability of fixation remains unchanged with frequency.
evidence: This is concluded from the simulation data and theoretical analysis

claim: The frequency threshold observed in earlier experiments is an artifact of limited experimental sampling rather than a frequency-dependent change in selective effect.
source: We conclude that the frequency threshold observed in earlier experiments is, therefore, an artifact of limited experimental sampling rather than a frequency-dependent change in selective effect.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, inferred from the simulation results and analysis of experimental design

claim: The simulations model asexual populations that mimic microbial evolution experiments under generally-accepted parameter values.
source: Our computer simulations (Raynes, 2019) model asexual populations that mimic microbial evolution experiments under generally-accepted parameter values (Raynes et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to the simulation code and parameter justification

claim: The simulations consider haploid asexual populations of constant size evolving in discrete, non-overlapping generations according to the Wright-Fisher model.
source: In brief, we consider haploid asexual populations of constant size, N, evolving in discrete, non-overlapping generations according to the Wright-Fisher model (Ewens, 2004).
evidence: This describes the simulation model, with citation to the Wright-Fisher model

claim: Populations in the simulations are composed of genetic lineages - subpopulations of individuals with the same genotype.
source: Populations are composed of genetic lineages - subpopulations of individuals with the same genotype.
evidence: This describes the structure of the simulation model

claim: A genotype in the simulations is modeled as an array of 99 fitness-affecting loci and 1 mutation rate modifier locus.
source: A genotype is modeled as an array of 99 fitness-affecting loci and 1 mutation rate modifier locus, which in a mutator state raises the genomic mutation rate m-fold.
evidence: This describes the genetic architecture in the simulation model

claim: The mutation rate modifier locus in a mutator state raises the genomic mutation rate m-fold.
source: A genotype is modeled as an array of 99 fitness-affecting loci and 1 mutation rate modifier locus, which in a mutator state raises the genomic mutation rate m-fold.
evidence: This describes how the mutator allele functions in the simulation

claim: In the simulations shown in Figure 1, beneficial mutations at fitness loci increase fitness by a constant effect s_ben, while deleterious mutations decrease fitness by a constant effect s_del.
source: For computational efficiency, simulations in Figure 1 assume constant fitness effects: beneficial mutations at the fitness loci increase fitness by a constant effect sben, while deleterious mutations decrease fitness by a constant effect sdel.
evidence: This describes the fitness model used in specific simulations

claim: In simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, beneficial and deleterious fitness effects are randomly drawn from an exponential distribution with mean s_ben = 0.1 and s_del = -0.1 respectively.
source: In simulations in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, beneficial and deleterious fitness effects are randomly drawn from an exponential distribution with the mean sben = 0.1 and sdel = -0.1 respectively.
evidence: This describes the fitness model used in alternative simulations

claim: Neither the strength nor the sign of selection on mutators depend on their initial frequency.
source: Here, we use stochastic, agent-based simulations to show that neither the strength nor the sign of selection on mutators depend on their initial frequency
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main finding

claim: While the overall probability of mutator hitchhiking increases predictably with frequency, the per-capita probability of fixation remains unchanged.
source: and while the overall probability of hitchhiking increases predictably with frequency, the per-capita probability of fixation remains unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main finding
